summary: Specifies the C language bindings for version 2, update 1 of the Generic Security Service API, which RFC 2743 describes at a conceptual level. It tells C programmers exact function and type names to use. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: GSS-API gives applications a common way to request authentication and message protection from different security mechanisms. RFC 2744 defines the C types and functions an application uses to call that interface.

questions: how to use gss-api in c
what is a gss-api security context
subtitle: The C types, functions, and status codes for the Generic Security Service API.

tldr.problem: RFC 2743 describes GSS-API without language-specific details, so C applications need agreed bindings for functions, data types, and constants.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2744 defines C function signatures, opaque handles, buffers, object identifiers, status codes, service flags, and the gssapi.h header file.
tldr.outcome: It specifies Version 2, Update 1 of the C bindings, obsoletes RFC 1509, and is updated by RFC 5896.

today: RFC 2744 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2000. It obsoletes RFC 1509 and is updated by RFC 5896.

sections.title: The GSS-API Process
sections.content:
The Generic Security Service Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) lets an application request security services without choosing one cryptographic mechanism in its application code. It can authenticate a peer, delegate rights, and provide per-message integrity or confidentiality.

Use proceeds through credentials, context establishment, message protection, and context deletion. During context establishment, the applications may exchange opaque tokens. The calling application transfers each token to the peer and passes received tokens to the matching GSS-API routine.
sections.plainLanguage: An application obtains credentials, exchanges tokens with its peer to establish a context, and then protects messages. Each side deletes its context when communication ends.

sections.title: Groups of C Routines
sections.content:
The C bindings organize routines into credential management, context management, per-message protection, name handling, and miscellaneous operations. Examples include gss_acquire_cred, gss_init_sec_context, gss_get_mic, gss_import_name, and gss_display_status.

Implementations may provide mechanism-specific routines when a generic routine cannot provide needed functionality. The RFC encourages applications to use generic routines where possible so that they remain portable across mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The API groups functions by task: credentials, contexts, protected messages, names, and status reporting. Generic functions help applications work across security mechanisms.

sections.title: C Types, Buffers, and Names
sections.content:
OM_uint32 is the unsigned integer type used for values that need at least 32 bits. A gss_buffer_desc holds a length and a pointer to bytes; the application releases returned buffer storage with gss_release_buffer. Credentials, names, and contexts use opaque handles, so applications do not inspect their internal representation.

Object identifiers select mechanisms and name types. GSS-API names can be held in an internal form or passed as a contiguous string with an identifier for its namespace. Channel bindings let the applications associate address and application data with a context; if the bindings differ, context establishment can fail with GSS_S_BAD_BINDINGS. Applications should not put confidential data in bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: Buffers carry a length and a pointer, while credential, name, and context handles hide internal details. Channel bindings let both applications check that they are establishing a context with the same channel information.

sections.title: Major and Mechanism Status Codes
sections.content:
Every routine reports a major GSS status and a mechanism-specific minor status. The major status is a 32-bit value: an 8-bit calling-error field, an 8-bit routine-error field, and 16 bits of supplementary information. A nonzero value in the upper 16 bits indicates a call error.

Supplementary information can report that context setup needs another token, or that a token is duplicate, old, out of sequence, or missing. The macros GSS_CALLING_ERROR(), GSS_ROUTINE_ERROR(), GSS_SUPPLEMENTARY_INFO(), and GSS_ERROR() let an application inspect the fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The major status separates errors in the call from errors in the routine and additional information. The minor status gives details specific to the underlying mechanism.

sections.title: Optional Context Services
sections.content:
The initiator can request services such as delegation, mutual authentication, replay detection, sequence detection, confidentiality, integrity, and anonymous authentication. The returned flags describe what the established context actually supports. If a mechanism cannot provide a requested service, it may continue without it, leaving the application to decide whether to proceed.

Delegation is only permitted when the application explicitly requests it. Context transfer between processes is optional; when supported, the exported token may contain cryptographic keys or other sensitive information, so the application must protect it. Some mechanisms allow message protection before context setup finishes, as reported by GSS_C_PROT_READY_FLAG.
sections.plainLanguage: The initiator requests services, then checks the returned flags to learn which ones the mechanism provides. The application must protect a context-transfer token because it may contain sensitive information.

sections.title: Establishing a Context
sections.content:
Context establishment can require one or more token exchanges. A portable application calls gss_init_sec_context or gss_accept_sec_context in a loop, sends any returned token, and calls again when the status includes GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED. The first call uses GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT; later calls use the returned context handle.

If a call fails after creating a partial context, the application should delete that context with gss_delete_sec_context. Once setup succeeds, the application can call per-message routines such as gss_wrap and gss_unwrap for integrity and, when available, confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep exchanging tokens until the status says context setup is complete. Then use the context to protect messages, and delete it when it is no longer needed.

sections.title: Security Depends on the Mechanism
sections.content:
Calling GSS-API does not by itself provide security or assurance. The underlying mechanism determines which services are available, so applications must check both the services they requested and the status and flags returned.

When an application transfers a context between processes, local controls should restrict access to the transfer token and its sensitive contents. The RFC includes the C header file that implementations should provide and additional notes about application binary portability.
sections.plainLanguage: The API is an interface to security mechanisms, not a security guarantee by itself. Applications must check what protection the selected mechanism actually provides.
